passage:
It was show-and-tell day at the kindergarten. Parveen held up a small box of sheer khurma. "On Eid, my Nani makes this. We wake up early, wear new clothes and go to everyone's house."
"Do all families do that?" asked a classmate.
Parveen thought. "This is how my family does it."
Vikas, the teacher, smiled. "Thank you, Parveen. Who else has a family festival?" Hands flew up.

qa.q: What did Parveen hold up at show-and-tell?
qa.a: She held up a small box of sheer khurma.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when the classmate asked if all families do that?
qa.a: She may have felt a little unsure at first, so she paused before answering that this is how her family does it.

qa.q: How did Vikas help the class learn from Parveen's share?
qa.a: He thanked her and invited others to share their family festivals.

qa.q: How might classmates feel after Parveen's story?
qa.a: They might feel curious and eager to share their own traditions.

grounding: It shows a child sharing a festival tradition and understanding it as her family's way.

passage: I'm Payal, and my cousin Hrithik is five. On Onam morning he helped Ammamma lay flowers for the pookalam in the courtyard. He carefully put yellow petals in the middle. "This is how we do it," he told me, very serious, "the yellow goes first." I'm not sure where he got that rule, but Ammamma nodded. Later, he sat still on the floor for the sadya and ate the payasam last, like the grown-ups.

qa.q: What colour petals did Hrithik put in the middle?
qa.a: He put yellow petals in the middle.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's serious "This is how we do it" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels proud and sure of his family's way of making the pookalam.

qa.q: How could Ammamma help Hrithik learn more about Onam?
qa.a: She could tell him a folk story about the festival while they make the pookalam.

qa.q: How does Payal see Hrithik's rule?
qa.a: Payal isn't sure where he got it, but notices Ammamma agrees with him.

grounding: An older cousin observes a child taking part in a festival tradition as his family's way.

It poured all Diwali evening, and the courtyard where Parul's family always made rangoli was a puddle. Parul, five, pressed her nose to the window.

"No rangoli this year?" she wailed.

Her big brother Ujjwal thought, then spread newspaper on the living room floor. "Our family always makes one. We'll just make it inside."

They used rice flour and turmeric. Parul pressed her small handprint in the middle, like Ma did every year.

"This is our Diwali way," she said, very proud.

qa.q: What did they use to make the rangoli indoors?
qa.a: They used rice flour and turmeric.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she saw the courtyard?
qa.a: She was upset and disappointed, pressing her nose to the window and wailing that there would be no rangoli.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped keep the tradition?
qa.a: He adapted the tradition by moving it indoors, showing that the family's way could continue despite the rain.

qa.q: How might Ma feel seeing Parul's handprint in the rangoli?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched that Parul copied her own yearly habit.

grounding: Shows a young child keeping a family festival tradition despite heavy rain, sensing 'this is our family's way'.

On Gurpurab morning in their Ludhiana home, Tejas, five, tied a small orange patka on his head, with Mummy's help.

"Why do we go to the gurdwara so early?" he asked.

"Because in our family we help cook the langar," Amandeep said. "Your Nanaji did it, and I did it."

In the langar hall, Tejas carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate. He copied the grown-ups, folding his hands. "Our family does this every year," he told the boy next to him.

qa.a: He carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate.

qa.a: Amandeep explained it as something the family has always done, naming Nanaji and Amandeep's own turn, so he could see his place in it.

qa.a: He may feel curious, or share his own family's ways in return.

grounding: Shows a young child joining a family festival custom and saying 'this is what our family does'.

“Amma, the milk is going to spill!”
“Let it, Hemant. Watch.”
The milk in the new clay pot rose, foamed, and bubbled over the edge.
Bhavna and Paati clapped. “Pongalo Pongal!”
Hemant, five, clapped too. “Why do we let it spill?”
“So our year overflows with good things. That's how our family does it.”
“Every year?”
“Every year. My Paati did it too.”
Hemant shouted it again, louder. “Pongalo Pongal!”

qa.q: What did the milk bubble over?
qa.a: It bubbled over the edge of the new clay pot.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when everyone clapped?
qa.a: He felt excited and happy to be part of the celebration.

qa.q: How could Bhavna help Hemant learn more about the tradition?
qa.a: She could tell him stories of how her Paati celebrated and let him help with the next step.

qa.q: How might Paati feel hearing Hemant shout “Pongalo Pongal”?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and happy that the family tradition continues.

grounding: A five-year-old takes part in a family Pongal ritual and learns why they do it.

Class note, February. Teacher: Ishita.
Today Pema (five) told the class about Losar, her family's new year. She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.
She showed us how her family says “Tashi Delek” with hands together. “That's how we say happy new year at home,” she said, standing very straight.
The other children tried saying it. Pema corrected them, giggling.
Next step: I've invited Pema's Ama to tell a folk story next week.

qa.q: What did Pema bring for the class?
qa.a: She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.

qa.q: How did Pema seem to feel sharing her tradition?
qa.a: She seemed proud and confident, standing very straight.

qa.q: Why is inviting Pema's Ama a good next step?
qa.a: It brings Pema's family tradition into the classroom and helps all children learn about it.

qa.q: How might the other children feel learning to say “Tashi Delek”?
qa.a: They probably feel curious and enjoy learning something new from their classmate.

grounding: A teacher notes a five-year-old sharing her family's Losar traditions with pride.

passage:
On Ugadi morning in their village near Hassan, Mohit-thatha handed Harsha, five, a little leaf cup.
“Bevu-bella,” he said. “Neem and jaggery.”
Harsha tasted it. His face scrunched. “Bitter! And sweet!”
Thatha laughed. “Yes. That's how our family starts the new year. A little bitter, a little sweet, because the year will have both.”
Harsha tasted again, slower. “Thatha, next year can I make it?”
“Next year, you'll grind the jaggery.”

qa.q: What did Mohit-thatha hand Harsha?
qa.a: He handed him a little leaf cup of bevu-bella.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when he tasted the bevu-bella?
qa.a: He was surprised by the bitter and sweet taste, then curious and keen to help.

qa.q: How did Thatha help Harsha understand the tradition?
qa.a: He explained the meaning simply and promised Harsha a job next year.

qa.q: How might Thatha feel when Harsha asks to make it next year?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and proud that Harsha wants to carry on the tradition.

grounding: A five-year-old takes part in an Ugadi tradition and learns what it means in his family.

In Oaxaca, Alejandro's family was building the altar for the Day of the Dead. His friend Kaito, visiting from next door, looked at the marigolds and the photos.
"Why is there bread for your grandpa? He can't eat it."
Alejandro placed the bread carefully. "This is how our family does it. We put his favourite things so he knows we remember."
"We light incense for my grandma," said Kaito.
Alejandro nodded. "Then you can help with the candles."
They lit them together while Alejandro's abuela hummed.

qa.q: What flowers were on the altar?
qa.a: Marigolds.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling as he placed the bread carefully?
qa.a: Alejandro felt proud and loving about his family's tradition and wanted to do it right.

qa.q: How could Alejandro's abuela help the boys learn more?
qa.a: She could tell them a short story about the grandpa in the photo while they finish the altar.

qa.q: How might Kaito feel when Alejandro invites him to help?
qa.a: Kaito is likely happy and included, since Kaito's own family's tradition was welcomed too.

grounding: A child in Mexico explains his family's Day of the Dead tradition to a friend.

The day after Makar Sankranti, the kindergarten had sharing time. Mahima held up a small jar of til-gud.
"We give these and say, 'Eat sweet, speak sweet.' That's what my family does."
Gargi put up her hand. "We make pongal and boil it over till it spills!"
"Why spill?" asked someone.
"Because that's how our family does it. It means lots of good things."
Mahima thought, then offered Gargi a til-gud. "Eat sweet, speak sweet."
Gargi took it and said it back, giggling.

qa.q: What did Mahima hold up at sharing time?
qa.a: A small jar of til-gud.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she offered Gargi a til-gud?
qa.a: Mahima felt proud of her family's custom and friendly towards Gargi.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on this sharing time?
qa.a: The teacher could invite other children to share their family's festival foods so everyone learns how different homes celebrate.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Mahima's custom?
qa.a: Gargi finds it fun and friendly, and happily joins in, even though her own family celebrates with pongal.

grounding: Children at school share how their families mark the winter harvest festival.

I'm Sunaina, Divyansh's big sister. During Durga Puja, we went to the pandal near our house.
Divyansh walked straight up to Dadu and touched his feet, then Dida's. Nobody told him to. He looked at me like he was waiting.
Then he put his hands together and bowed to the idol, just like Dida does.
Later, a boy from his class laughed. "Why did you do that?"
Divyansh said, "That's what our family does," and went back to eating his bhog.
I don't know if he understands it all. But he looked very sure.

qa.q: Whom did Divyansh walk straight up to first?
qa.a: Dadu.

qa.q: What does Divyansh's steady answer to the boy suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed calm and proud of his family's way, and wasn't upset by being laughed at.

qa.q: How could Sunaina support Divyansh after the boy laughed?
qa.a: Sunaina could tell him she noticed how he respected Dadu and Dida and that every family has its own customs.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Divyansh at the pandal?
qa.a: Sunaina isn't sure how much he understands, but she sees him as very sure and at home in the family's traditions.

On Losar morning the snow was so thick that Pema's father couldn't reach the monastery for the festival prayers. Pema, five, cried. "But we always go!"
Her grandmother Leela lit butter lamps at home. "Then today we pray here. The prayers are the same."
She taught Pema to fold her hands and bow three times. Then they ate the special noodles and Leela told the old story of the new year.
Pema bowed three times again before bed, on her own.

qa.q: Why couldn't Pema's father reach the monastery?
qa.a: The snow was so thick.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when they couldn't go?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, crying "But we always go!"

qa.q: How did Leela keep the tradition going?
qa.a: She lit butter lamps at home, taught Pema the bows, and told the old story.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when Pema bows before bed on her own?
qa.a: Leela likely feels warm and proud that Pema has made the tradition her own.

grounding: Shows a young child participating in a family festival tradition despite an obstacle.

During the Durga Puja holidays in their Kolkata flat, Jahnavi, five, sat on her uncle Manoj's lap while he told the story of the goddess fighting the buffalo demon.
"Again!" she said.
He told it again. She acted out the fight with a spoon.
That evening at the pandal, she pointed at the idol. "That's her! In our family we tell her story every year."
Manoj smiled. "Yes, we do."

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel at the pandal?

qa.a: Manoj likely feels happy and touched that she feels part of the tradition.

"Why do we put the lamps on the steps, Paati?" asked Vasudha, six, as they lit little clay lamps for Karthigai Deepam.
"Because this is how our family does it. My grandmother did it, then me, then your Amma."
"Meera's family doesn't do it."
"Meera's family has Christmas lights, no? Every family has its own ways."
Her cousin Karthik came up the stairs carrying more lamps. "Can I light one too?"
"Only if Vasudha shows you how," Paati said.
Vasudha stood tall. "Hold the lamp like this. Slowly. It's our family way."

qa.q: What does Meera's family have, according to Paati?
qa.a: Meera's family has Christmas lights.

qa.q: What does Vasudha standing tall suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and important, trusted to show her cousin the family tradition.

qa.q: How could Paati keep helping Vasudha understand family traditions?
qa.a: She could keep telling stories of who did it before and let Vasudha lead small parts, while showing respect for other families' ways too.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel being taught by Vasudha?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels excited and included, getting to light a lamp and join the family ritual.

grounding: Shows a young child joining a family festival tradition and understanding that it is how her family does things.
